Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., talk to reporters about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) The U.S. Senate is considering a nearly-500 page bipartisan permitting reform bill that has divided clean energy groups, environmental organizations, and climate action advocates. Here’s how prominent organizations and individuals are lining up on each side of the debate.  Five BAAJA supporters and noted individuals in favor of the bill Citizens Climate Lobby “For too long, an outdated and inefficient permitting system has slowed the clean energy projects and transmission infrastructure we need to cut emissions and build a cleaner, more reliable energy system.” 2. AFL-CIO and other labor unions “The changes put forward in the permitting bill will allow our nation to build new and clean energy generation as more of our economy runs on electricity; slash the time it takes to build transmission lines; cut the emissions that cause climate change; and control household costs.” 3. 300 solar and energy storage companies via the Solar Energy Industries Association “Solar energy and storage technology are the fastest and most affordable new electricity resources to deploy. However, the current system of permitting limits the speedy deployment of clean, lower cost solar and storage. Solar and storage developers cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid. In the end, these delays cost American families in higher utility bills.” 4. American Petroleum Institute and leaders from across the oil and natural gas industry Maryann Mannen, Chairman, President, and CEO of Marathon Petroleum: “This transformative legislation will help unleash energy infrastructure development and reduce legal barriers for project development, including oil and gas pipeline expansion. … As this legislation demonstrates, it is possible to protect our air, land, and water without sacrificing our ability to expand and improve our nation’s energy infrastructure, which safely and efficiently moves the products that make modern life possible.” We can't do this work without you. Electric companies via The Edison Electric Institute, which represents all U.S. investor-owned electric companies “America needs to build energy infrastructure faster to meet growing electricity demand, strengthen reliability, support economic growth, and make electricity more affordable for customers. A more predictable and efficient permitting process is an important part of meeting that challenge.” Noted individuals in the climate space: Bill sponsor Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island; climate scientist Zeke Hausfather; “Volts” podcast host, David Roberts “Nobody likes it when I say this but it’s true so I’ll say it again: there is no ‘better deal’ on permitting in the next Congress, for very simple reasons that are accessible to everyone. If you think the status quo is preferable to a permitting compromise, just be honest and say so.” – David Roberts on Bluesky Five BAAJA opponents and noted individuals opposed to the bill 1. 11 tribal organizations , including the Native American Rights Fund, National Indian Child Welfare Association, and the National Congress of American Indians “Despite claims that the revised legislation responds to Tribal concerns, the proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act in Title III of BAAJA continue to fundamentally undermine Tribal sovereignty, weaken longstanding federal protections, fail to ensure meaningful government-to-government Tribal consultation, and threaten sacred sites and cultural resources.” 2. The Sierra Club “Updating and expediting transmission and clean energy permitting is essential to delivering lower costs, reduced air, water, and climate pollution, protecting communities, and expanding the grid for the American people. But rushing legislation that erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities, abandons clean water safeguards, and wildlife protections, while further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy and our public lands is not an acceptable outcome.” 3. NAACP “The NAACP strongly opposes BAAJA because we should not rush through a decision that directly threatens the health, safety, and future of Black and frontline communities. This bill puts our community and our planet’s health in the hands of billionaires and their interests. We refuse to let our future be determined by corporate polluters and people who seem more aligned with them than people who live in sacrifice zones.” 4. The Climate Justice Alliance “If passed, this legislation will benefit the largest fossil fuel polluters, explode the approval of data centers, and enrich tech billionaires, entrenching communities with more pollution, harm, and higher bills.” 5. NRDC   “While NRDC supports the elements of the bill that would help accelerate needed transmission and grid modernization, the bill goes too far in weakening essential environmental safeguards and opportunities for public participation. We oppose the bill as written.”  Noted individuals: Al Gore, conservation expert and writer Ayana Elizabeth Johnson, climate scientist Michael Mann, environmentalist and author Bill McKibben, and actor Mark Ruffalo. “I think that if this deal had been made thirty years ago, it might have made sense—we’d be reaping the benefits now. But the fossil fuel industry made sure we didn’t. And this bill, which they’re backing with great enthusiasm, seems an awful lot like a hedge to make sure they can string their business model out for a few more decades—a way to lock in the fruits of their decades of political obstructionism. Gambling on something better is indeed a gamble—maybe the political moment will never come again. But gambling that these kind of reductions are anywhere near sufficient is not a gamble against politics. It’s a gamble against physics,” Bill McKibben wrote on Substack. BAAJA: Who’s in favor and who’s opposed?

by Samantha Harrington, Yale Climate Connections
November 18, 2026

The U.S. Senate is considering a nearly-500 page bipartisan permitting reform bill that has divided clean energy groups, environmental organizations, and climate action advocates. Here’s how prominent organizations and individuals are lining up on each side of the debate. 

Five BAAJA supporters and noted individuals in favor of the bill

  1. Citizens Climate Lobby

“For too long, an outdated and inefficient permitting system has slowed the clean energy projects and transmission infrastructure we need to cut emissions and build a cleaner, more reliable energy system.”

2. AFL-CIO and other labor unions

“The changes put forward in the permitting bill will allow our nation to build new and clean energy generation as more of our economy runs on electricity; slash the time it takes to build transmission lines; cut the emissions that cause climate change; and control household costs.”

3. 300 solar and energy storage companies via the Solar Energy Industries Association

“Solar energy and storage technology are the fastest and most affordable new electricity resources to deploy. However, the current system of permitting limits the speedy deployment of clean, lower cost solar and storage. Solar and storage developers cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid. In the end, these delays cost American families in higher utility bills.”

4. American Petroleum Institute and leaders from across the oil and natural gas industry

Maryann Mannen, Chairman, President, and CEO of Marathon Petroleum: “This transformative legislation will help unleash energy infrastructure development and reduce legal barriers for project development, including oil and gas pipeline expansion. … As this legislation demonstrates, it is possible to protect our air, land, and water without sacrificing our ability to expand and improve our nation's energy infrastructure, which safely and efficiently moves the products that make modern life possible.”

5. Electric companies via The Edison Electric Institute, which represents all U.S. investor-owned electric companies

“America needs to build energy infrastructure faster to meet growing electricity demand, strengthen reliability, support economic growth, and make electricity more affordable for customers. A more predictable and efficient permitting process is an important part of meeting that challenge.”

Noted individuals in the climate space: Bill sponsor Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island; climate scientist Zeke Hausfather; “Volts” podcast host, David Roberts

“Nobody likes it when I say this but it's true so I'll say it again: there is no ‘better deal’ on permitting in the next Congress, for very simple reasons that are accessible to everyone. If you think the status quo is preferable to a permitting compromise, just be honest and say so.” - David Roberts on Bluesky

Five BAAJA opponents and noted individuals opposed to the bill

1. 11 tribal organizations, including the Native American Rights Fund, National Indian Child Welfare Association, and the National Congress of American Indians

“Despite claims that the revised legislation responds to Tribal concerns, the proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act in Title III of BAAJA continue to fundamentally undermine Tribal sovereignty, weaken longstanding federal protections, fail to ensure meaningful government-to-government Tribal consultation, and threaten sacred sites and cultural resources.”

2. The Sierra Club

“Updating and expediting transmission and clean energy permitting is essential to delivering lower costs, reduced air, water, and climate pollution, protecting communities, and expanding the grid for the American people. But rushing legislation that erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities, abandons clean water safeguards, and wildlife protections, while further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy and our public lands is not an acceptable outcome.”

3. NAACP

“The NAACP strongly opposes BAAJA because we should not rush through a decision that directly threatens the health, safety, and future of Black and frontline communities. This bill puts our community and our planet's health in the hands of billionaires and their interests. We refuse to let our future be determined by corporate polluters and people who seem more aligned with them than people who live in sacrifice zones.”

4. The Climate Justice Alliance

“If passed, this legislation will benefit the largest fossil fuel polluters, explode the approval of data centers, and enrich tech billionaires, entrenching communities with more pollution, harm, and higher bills.”

5. NRDC 

“While NRDC supports the elements of the bill that would help accelerate needed transmission and grid modernization, the bill goes too far in weakening essential environmental safeguards and opportunities for public participation. We oppose the bill as written.” 

Noted individuals: Al Gore, conservation expert and writer Ayana Elizabeth Johnson, climate scientist Michael Mann, environmentalist and author Bill McKibben, and actor Mark Ruffalo.

“I think that if this deal had been made thirty years ago, it might have made sense—we’d be reaping the benefits now. But the fossil fuel industry made sure we didn’t. And this bill, which they’re backing with great enthusiasm, seems an awful lot like a hedge to make sure they can string their business model out for a few more decades—a way to lock in the fruits of their decades of political obstructionism.

Gambling on something better is indeed a gamble—maybe the political moment will never come again. But gambling that these kind of reductions are anywhere near sufficient is not a gamble against politics. It’s a gamble against physics,” Bill McKibben wrote on Substack.

Sara Peach contributed reporting.
